title: A Method to Study the Correlation Between Local Collagen Structure and Mechanical Properties of Atherosclerotic Plaque Fibrous Tissue
protocol: Collect fresh human carotid atherosclerotic plaque specimens from consenting patients who underwent carotid endarterectomy surgery.
Remove blood remnants using phosphate-buffered saline (1x PBS).
Dry the specimen with a gauze pad.
Place the specimen in a 15 mL tube using tweezers.
Snap-freeze the tissue by placing the tube in liquid nitrogen for 10 min.
Store the sample in a -80 °C freezer until the day of µCT imaging.
Take the plaque specimen out of the 15 mL tube.
If necessary, fill the tube with PBS to free the tissue from the tube walls.
Leave the tissue in PBS until it can be removed easily.
Dry the plaque specimen thoroughly using tissue paper.
Turn on the µCT system by pressing the green button.
Press warm up in the CT software and wait 15 minutes.
Manually place an X-ray filter of Cu 0.06 mm + Al 0.5 mm into the µCT system.
Select the folder for storing images.
Choose a scanning time of 4 min, resolution of 172 µm, voltage of 90 kV, amperage of 88 mA, field of view of 86 mm, and rotation of 360° in the software parameters panel.
Open the door of the device manually.
Pull out the platform and place parafilm on it.
Place the sample on the platform towards its further extreme end.
Manually insert the platform back into the device and close the door.
Activate live mode (eye icon) to view and adjust the sample position in real-time.
Move the platform with arrow keys to center the sample within the field of view.
Start imaging using the button located at the bottom-middle of the software interface.
Once imaging is complete, press the door icon at the bottom under the abort button to open the device door.
Snap-freeze the plaque specimen as described in step 1.1.3 after µCT scanning.
Store the snap-frozen specimen at -80 °C until it is needed for multiphoton microscopy imaging or mechanical testing.
Open the acquired DICOM files in 3D Slicer software.
Go to Segment editor.
Select create a new segmentation | the volume to be analyzed as a master volume.
Click on Add to add a segment.
Press its name and color to change these parameters.
To define the segments, click on effects | threshold in the bottom part of the window.
Use this threshold tool to differentiate between calcified (>450 HU) and non-calcified (<450 HU) tissue regions.
Once the threshold is selected, press Apply in the bottom part.
Press Show 3D (just to the right of Add) to visualize the segmentation in the 3D view.
If there are areas of the segmentation that are not desired, remove them with the scissors effect.
Change the opacity of segments in the segmentation module by clicking on the name of the desired segmentation.
Thaw the plaque by submersion in PBS at room temperature for approximately 10 min.
Open the 3D construction of the plaque created in steps 1.2.13-1.2.18 in the 3D slicer software.
Identify which parts of the 3D reconstruction correspond to the real plaque sample using natural landmarks.
Visually identify an area of the 3D reconstruction that does not contain calcifications.
Cut the plaque open along the longitudinal axis of the artery using surgical scissors and tweezers.
Start from a pre-existing cut if present for optimal tissue usage.
Exclude samples without a clear tubular shape or defined longitudinal direction.
Cut out rectangular test samples from the plaque specimens to maximize size while avoiding tears or calcifications.
Ensure that the test samples have a width-to-length (WL) ratio of <1 in the gauge length once mounted in the tensile tester.
Divide 40 g of silicone elastomer base over two 50 mL tubes.
Add 2 g of curing agent to each tube using a Pasteur pipet.
Mix the components with the pipet.
Centrifuge the tubes for 1 min at 700 × g.
Fill a Petri dish (10 cm diameter) with a thin layer (approximately 0.5-1 cm) of silicon.
Incubate the Petri dish in an oven at 65 °C for 3 h or place it at room temperature for 48 h.
Fix both ends of a plaque test sample to the silicon by pinning needles in the tissue.
Ensure the luminal side of the sample is facing upward.
Insert needles in the region of the sample that will be in the clamps of the tensile testing device during mechanical testing.
Put on safety glasses.
Use a side cutter to shorten the needles so they stick out less than a few millimeters above the sample surface.
Fill the Petri dish with PBS until the sample is submerged.
Ensure a proper objective, optimized for infrared light and magnification of 20x, is mounted on the multiphoton microscope.
Start up the microscope system.
Open the operating software of the microscope.
Push back the microscope condenser arm and lower the objective to its lowest position.
Activate the multiphoton laser.
Place a Petri dish with the test sample underneath the objective.
Immerse the objective slightly in PBS, adding more PBS if necessary.
Set the light wavelength to 880 nm.
Turn off the multiphoton laser and activate the brightfield mode of the microscope.
Turn on the live scan mode.
Position the stage so that the objective is above the sample surface.
Bring the sample surface into focus.
Turn off the live scan mode.
Change the zoom factor to 1 under the acquisition tab.
Change the scan speed to 400 Hz under the acquisition tab.
Set the line average to 1 under the acquisition tab.
Configure the resolution to 128 x 128 pixels per image under the acquisition tab.
Click the raster pattern symbol in the first panel of the acquisition tab.
Wait for a tile scan panel to appear and turn on live scan mode.
Move the objective to a corner of the sample using the knobs on the smart panel.
Mark the position in the tile scan panel by clicking the mark position symbol.
Repeat marking positions for each corner of the sample.
Observe the appearance of a grid with orange tiles indicating all selected areas for imaging.
Toggle off the auto-stitching function.
Click start to create a tile scan of the entire sample surface.
Note the x- and y-coordinates of the upper left corner of each tile after completing the tile scan.
Observe the number of tiles in the x- and y- directions in the box called scanfield.
Note the size of the tile scan in the spreadsheet.
Calculate the coordinates of other tiles by adding/subtracting 739 µm.
Select tiles to be imaged with SHG imaging from the tile scan.
Avoid tiles that will be in the clamps during selection.
Leave one tile between each selected tile in both longitudinal and circumferential directions.
Turn off the lights in the room.
Cover the microscope stage with blackout fabric to prevent light reaching the detector.
Turn on the multiphoton (MP) laser.
Select the non-descanned detection (NDD) detector equipped with a 430-450 nm bandpass filter.
Identify the location of tiles to be imaged using information from step 2.3.10.
Fill in the coordinates in designated boxes and click enter so the objective moves to the right tile.
Turn on the live scan mode.
Increase the MP laser power by using the slider in the upper panel under beam path settings to get the highest possible laser power without significant bleaching.

Adjust the detector gain to obtain bright images, but without saturated pixels, by using the knob on the smart panel or by clicking on the name of the detector under beam path settings | additional channels.
Use the z-position knob on the smart panel to adjust the focus plane.
Move to the top of the sample and set the positions of the top of the z-stack by clicking on the arrowhead in the z-stack panel (under the acquisition tab | 3rd panel).
Focus on the sample until the SHG signal is no longer detected-this is the end of the stack.
Again, click on the arrowhead in the z-stack panel to set this position.
Turn off the live scan mode.
Keep the scan speed at 400 Hz under the acquisition tab.
Set the line average to 2 in the dropdown list.
Set the resolution to 512 x 512 pixels per image (pixel size of ~1.4 µm x 1.4 µm).
Toggle on the bidirectional X scanning button.
Fill a z-step size of 3 µm in the z-stack panel.
Click start in the bottom-right corner of the screen to create a z-stack.
Save the coordinates of the tile in the file name or give each tile its own number.
Make the horizontal tensile testing setup ready for usage, following the instructions for the tensile tester.
Attach two-sided foam tape to the inner faces of the clamps of the tensile tester and sandpaper to the inner side of the foam tape.
Place the heating bath in position.
Fill the heating bath with PBS up to the level of the bottom face of the clamps.
Turn the power source of the heating bath on and set the temperature to around 37 °C.
Mount the high-speed camera above the tensile testing system using a laboratory stand.
Mount a lens with a focal length of 50 mm on the camera through an extension ring.
Adjust the focus to ensure that the clamps are in focus.
Ensure the field of view is large enough to record the sample during the entire stretching procedure (FOV width: ± the sample width; FOV length: ± 2x the sample length).
Mount the lighting system above the tensile testing system using a laboratory stand.
Turn the lighting system on and adjust the light intensity and location to avoid reflections on the PBS surface in the camera image.
Adjust the exposure time and gain of the camera to obtain clear images.
Set the image acquisition software to capture at 30 frames/s at a resolution of 5.2 MP.

Set the displacement speed of one of the clamps such that the global engineering strain rate during mechanical testing is similar to the in vivo physiological straining rate of the tissue (5%/s for plaque tissue).
Dry the sample by lightly dabbing it with tissue paper.
Put the black tissue dye in the intended bucket of the airbrush.
Connect the airbrush to the compressor.
Turn on the airbrush compressor and set the pressure to 25 PSI.
Create an optimal speckle pattern on paper before spraying on the tissue.
Spray until a black/white ratio of 50:50 is met.
Move the needle of the airbrush back and forth to adjust the roughness of the speckle pattern.
Hold the airbrush approximately 30 cm away from the test sample and spray on the luminal surface.
Let the dye bond to the sample for 1 min at room temperature before submerging in PBS.
Place the sample in the clamps of the tensile tester with the circumferential direction aligned with the stretching direction.
Set the initial gauge length such that the WL ratio of the strips is less than 1.
Tighten the screws of the grips by applying a torque of 20 cNm using a torque screwdriver.
Visually inspect the sample for tears.
Introduce more PBS into the heating bath until the sample is submerged.
Wait until the temperature of the PBS reaches 37 °C again.
Acquire a calibration image with the high-speed camera, including the test sample and ruler as reference.
Ensure the ruler is at the same distance from the camera objective as the luminal surface of the sample.
Tare the load cell.
Start recording global force and displacement measurements from the load cell and actuator of the tensile tester.
Apply a prestretch of 0.05 N to remove slack in the sample.
Perform 10 cycles of preconditioning up to 10% strain based on gauge length measurement by the actuator after applying prestretch.
Start uniaxial tensile testing until complete failure of the sample, while recording video with high-speed camera.
After tissue failure, stop recording global force and displacement measurements.
Remove the test sample from the tensile testing device and discard appropriately.
Replace sandpaper and foam tape on clamps when preparing to test the next sample.
Open z-stacks obtained during MPM with SHG in ImageJ.
Create maximum intensity projections (MIPs) of each z-stack.
Analyze each MIP using FOA tool to measure collagen fiber orientation angles.
Set scales parameter as [3 4 5] or [2 4 6], based on vessel diameter.
Adjust vesselness threshold to 0.999, 0.9995, or 0.9999 depending on SHG signal intensity.
Fit a Gaussian distribution to the angle distribution histogram using FibLab tool.
Extract predominant fiber angle (µp) from the Gaussian distribution plot in MATLAB workspace.
Determine standard deviation (σp) of the fiber angle distribution.
Calculate anisotropic fraction (Pani = 1 − Piso) based on peak and baseline areas.
Perform visual inspection on camera images to identify the frame where rupture initiation occurs.
Visually identify the rupture location on this frame.
Inspect camera images for any crack or tear at the rupture site before mechanical testing starts.
Exclude samples from analysis if a tear is present at the rupture site.
Use Ncorr (v1.2) software for digital image correlation analysis.
Select the last frame before final stretching until failure as the reference image.
Choose all frames from the start of final stretching until just before rupture initiation as current images.
Define the sample surface as the region of interest, excluding areas near clamps by approximately 1 mm.
Perform DIC analysis with subset radius set to 30 pixels and spacing at three pixels.
Set iteration cutoff to 50 and norm of difference vector cutoff to 10^-5.
Use strain radius of 5 pixels and enable auto propagation with step number set to 5.
Obtain Green-Lagrange strain distributions of the ROI using DIC analysis with Ncorr.
Calculate the average Green-Lagrange strain of the entire plaque sample surface at the last frame before rupture.
Determine the Green-Lagrange strain at the rupture location.
Identify the rupture location on the reference image using natural landmarks and applied speckles in the test sample.
Overlay the reference image and tile scan to identify the rupture location on the tile scan.
Locate the MPM-SHG tile where the rupture occurred.
If the rupture is not in an MPM-SHG-scanned tile, identify the closest tile to the rupture location.
Obtain structural parameters from the tile where the rupture occurred.
